searches.note: Twenty eight searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's. Searches 4 and 6 (Te Koko's devising) served Cloudy Bay, Dog Point and Greywacke and are counted under Dog Point; search 13 (the 85 per cent rule) served every label and is counted under Brancott. Nine were restricted to one house's or one body's domain (cloudybay.com twice, dogpoint.co.nz four times, greywacke.com, frommwinery.co.nz, brancottestate.com, and the Ministry for Primary Industries with New Zealand Winegrowers once); the rest kept out the house's domain or Wikipedia where the author had leant on them. The first commit message of this check said twenty eight when twenty seven had been spent; the twenty eighth, on Brancott's making, followed it. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a beat was in no source of this check and rested on one account of the author's, it was cut or said with less; a house's claim about itself is hedged as its account.

Writers' own sites met among the results (Wine with Seth, Wine Anorak, a sommelier's newsletter, a Friday Red newsletter, two critics' tasting sites, Jancis Robinson's) are cited neither in the fragment nor as a source here; an address naming a living person (a merchant's Fromm page, a Rural News profile, The Wine Society's grower story) is used for nothing it alone says.

Serving temperatures were held to the service reference: the two young Sauvignons at 8 to 10 and 7 to 10, the two barrel fermented at 10 to 12, the Pinot Noir at 15 to 17 like the other Pinot records of the wave.

tested: The first vintage of 1985 made in Gisborne from bought Marlborough fruit (search 1, the house's domain kept out): forty tonnes of Corbans' Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc from the Stoneleigh vineyard on Rapaura Road, picked at night and trucked north (The Drinks Business, Decanter); Decanter names Selaks' Gisborne winery, New Zealand Winegrowers' profile of 2026 names Corbans; Corbans supplied grapes and made wines for the first three years. The record's another company's winery stands; which one is open.

The founder's tasting of 1983 and the founding of 1985 (search 2, the house and Wikipedia kept out): Wine Searcher's guide, Majestic and Decanter agree. Confirmed, the house's account hedged as it is.

Veuve Clicquot's stake and full ownership: 1990 by Decanter's timeline and most accounts, 1991 by The Drinks Business, the early 1990s by Wine Spectator; full ownership in 2003 by all. The start of the 1990s and 2003 stand.

Te Koko (search 3 and two shared): first made in 1996 by the International Wine Challenge and Decanter, first released in 2000 by the house, wild yeast trials from 1991 and barrels set aside in 1992 by the house; the name from Te Koko o Kupe, the oyster dredge of Kupe, in the house's own words. Confirmed; the trials are not added.

The making (search 14, the house's domain): the 2025 note has eighty portions tasted and sixty one kept, about 1.8 per cent fermented warmer in large oak vats and a wild yeast portion; 2024 about 1.5 per cent; 2020 about four per cent in old barriques and vats. A few per cent or less stands; eighty or more refuted.

The ageing and the serve: the house's pages say it would age at least ten years and ages gracefully for a decade or more; serve at 8 to 10 degrees Celsius. Confirmed, and within the service reference for a light white.

The sites (search 25, the house's domain): Rapaura, Renwick and the Brancott Valley, called subregions of the Wairau Valley, with the Estate, Motukawa, Widow's Block, Red Shed and Mustang vineyards among the blocks. Confirmed.
Pelorus of 1987 (search 27, the house kept out): Wine Searcher's guide and a portfolio timeline give 1987, named for the dolphin Pelorus Jack. Confirmed.

The label: New Zealand's 85 per cent rule for a region and a grape (search 13, shared, the Ministry for Primary Industries) confirmed; James Cook's dates and the naming of 1770 stand on the author's sources and general record. Rules: nobody living named (the founder and the founding winemaker are described), no price, no score, nothing volatile, British, no dash. The questions: one key each, distractors of one kind, the explanations teach.

tested: The planting of 1973 (searches 9 and 12, New Zealand Winegrowers and Wikipedia kept out in the first): Wine Marlborough's timeline gives planting from 30 July to 3 August with the official celebration on 24 August; its history page and Destination Marlborough date the first vines to 11 August, shrouded in secrecy; The Press of 1978 has two hundred at the planting ceremony of 24 August 1973; New Zealand Winegrowers keeps 24 August as the planting. The crowd of press and politicians is not in any source read here and sits ill with the secrecy; refuted and rewritten.

The government scientist and the deposit: no result named a scientist of the research department; Wine Marlborough has the founder's son send his viticulturist to meet a land agent, and its timeline titles the step Montana purchases land. Rewritten to that.

The family from Dalmatia (search 10): Wikipedia has the first vines of 1934 in the Waitakere Ranges west of Auckland and the sons' company of 1961; another account has a son move a winery from Titirangi to Marlborough. Oratia is in no result; cut.

Sauvignon Blanc at Brancott in 1975 and the first commercial Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc of 1979 (search 11): 1975 by Stuff, Rural News and the region record; 1979 by Wine Marlborough, New Zealand Winegrowers and two merchants, 1980 for a first bottling by Rural News. Neither the replacing of the first vines nor Pinot Noir in 1975 was found; cut.
The West Auckland Sauvignon Blanc of 1969: New Zealand Winegrowers' fast facts give Waimauku in 1969, Stuff the cutting's arrival in 1970. Hedged as the national body's account.

New Zealand's 85 per cent rule (search 13): the Ministry for Primary Industries' labelling page confirms it for a variety, a vintage or an area, and for any combination of them; Chile's 75 per cent at home was not tested and is cut from the explanation.

The making (search 28, the house's domain kept out): the house's sheet for 2023 in the national catalogue has the grapes crushed and gently bag pressed, the juice promptly clarified to tank and a slow, cool fermentation; a German importer's sheet has steel and no oak. The words are set to the sheet's.
The other wines (search 24, the house's domain): Letter Series B from chosen Marlborough vineyards, Flight Song picked earlier for less alcohol. Confirmed.

Allied Domecq in 2001, Pernod Ricard in 2005 and the worldwide name of 2010 stand on the author's sources, not retested. Rules: the family and the viticulturist are not named, nothing volatile (the reported sale of 2025 stays out), British, no dash. Questions: one key each; the story question's distractors are of one kind.

changed.was: The company began in West Auckland, where a family from Dalmatia bought land at Oratia in the Waitakere Ranges and planted a vineyard, and two sons of that family later set up Montana Wines. In the early 1970s, on the advice of a scientist of the government's research department, Montana put a deposit on farmland on the Wairau Plains of Marlborough. On 24 August 1973, before a crowd of press, politicians and business leaders, it planted the Brancott Vineyard: the day, as New Zealand's wine body tells it, that Marlborough's wine industry was born. In 1975 some of the first vines were replaced with Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir, and in 1979 came the first commercial Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc, the start of the style the region is known for. Allied Domecq bought Montana in 2001, and Pernod Ricard took over Allied Domecq in 2005. From 2010 the brand took the name Brancott Estate across the world: the name of that first vineyard, and the name its wines already carried in the United States, where Montana is a state. For a sommelier, this is the bottle at the root of Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc.
changed.now: The company began in West Auckland, where a family from Dalmatia planted a vineyard, and two sons of that family later set up Montana Wines. In the early 1970s Montana sent its viticulturist south to find land and bought farmland on the Wairau Plains of Marlborough. Planting began in the winter of 1973, and on 24 August the company marked it with a ceremony at the Brancott Vineyard: the day, as New Zealand's wine body tells it, that Marlborough's wine industry was born. Sauvignon Blanc went in at Brancott in 1975, and in 1979 came the first commercial Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc, the start of the style the region is known for. Allied Domecq bought Montana in 2001, and Pernod Ricard took over Allied Domecq in 2005. From 2010 the brand took the name Brancott Estate across the world: the name of that first vineyard, and the name its wines already carried in the United States, where Montana is a state. For a sommelier, this is the bottle at the root of Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc.
changed.why: Planting began before 24 August by every account (30 July to 3 August, or 11 August), and 24 August was the ceremony; the scientist, the deposit, Oratia, the replacing of the first vines and the Pinot Noir of 1975 were in no source of this check.

tested: The founders (search 5, the house's domain): the couple are early Marlborough pioneers who planted grapes in the late 1970s; at Cloudy Bay the viticulturist met a winemaker and the two shaped the brand; the label was launched in February 2004 with fruit of 2002. Confirmed, except Dog Point Road, which no result gave for the 1970s land; cut.

Te Koko (searches 4 and 6, shared with Cloudy Bay and Greywacke): Cloudy Bay's own history credits the idea to its winemaker of 1991 to 2002 and his colleague, the founding winemaker; the year of creation varies (1996, 2000, 2001) by account. Kept, hedged as Cloudy Bay's account. The same searches found that this winemaker, a Dog Point founder, died in early 2026 (The Drinks Business, Wine Marlborough).

Section 94 (searches 7, 8 and 26): a single parcel planted in 1992, hand picked, whole bunch pressed, fermented and aged in older French oak for eighteen months and bottled without fining, by the house's 2021 page; the name from an early or colonial survey by Grape Collective, The Wine Society, Flatiron, Vinography and Wine Anorak; the subdivision of the vast Hawkesbury Run in the house's own words, quoted by Wine List Australia; local history confirms the Hawkesbury run of the first settlers. Kept, hedged as the house's account; the making set to eighteen months in all.

The name Dog Point (search 20, the house's domain): boundary dogs strayed, bred into a wild pack and were removed by settlers, in the house's words. Kept as the house's story; no independent account was sought.
Organic growing: conversion from 2009 and BioGro certification by the house's organics page. The year is added, hedged.

The other wines (searches 21 and 23): the house counts four wines, a Sauvignon Blanc and three barrel fermented with natural yeasts; its Chardonnay is whole bunch pressed into French oak with wild primary and malolactic fermentation over eighteen months; its Pinot Noir ferments in small open top steel fermenters and is then pressed to French oak for eighteen months. The Chardonnay note had the Pinot Noir fermented in barrel; refuted and rewritten. The classic Sauvignon's own making was not found in a sheet (one listing has it fermented entirely with indigenous yeast), so the note says only what the house's count implies, hedged.

The serve of 10 to 12 degrees Celsius sits within full whites; the ageing and the glass are the author's gathering of importer notes and are left. Rules: both founding couples, the son and the winemaker are described, never named; no price, no score; nothing volatile (the largest organic vineyard claim stays out); British, no dash. Questions: one key each.

changed.was: As the house tells it, the place took its name from the early sheep runs: boundary dogs lost by shepherds bred into a wild pack that preyed on the flocks they were meant to guard, until settlers cleared them, and the spot became Dog Point. In the late 1970s a Marlborough couple bought land on Dog Point Road and planted their first vines. The husband became Cloudy Bay's viticulturist, and there he worked beside one of its winemakers, who with a colleague devised Te Koko, Cloudy Bay's wild fermented, barrel aged Sauvignon Blanc. A single parcel of the vineyard was planted in 1992, and it carries its title from an early survey of Marlborough, made when the vast Hawkesbury Run was cut up: Section 94. The two couples made their first wine of their own from the 2002 vintage and launched the Dog Point label in February 2004, and Section 94 brought the barrel and the wild yeast to a parcel of their own. The vineyard was later turned over to organic growing and is certified organic. For a sommelier, Section 94 is the bottle to offer when a guest wants Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc with texture rather than snap.

changed.was: Greywacke, said GREY-wack-ee, is the name of New Zealand's most abundant bedrock, a hard grey sandstone whose rounded stones lie in the region's riverbeds. Its founder came to Marlborough as the founding winemaker of Cloudy Bay and directed that house's first twenty five vintages from 1985, the years in which Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc became known across the world. At Cloudy Bay, by that house's account, he and a colleague devised Te Koko, a Sauvignon Blanc fermented with wild yeast and aged in barrel, first made in 1996. In 2009 he and his wife set up a label of their own, buying much of its fruit from the vineyards of one of Dog Point's founding families, his former colleagues at Cloudy Bay. Wild Sauvignon follows the same thinking: wild yeasts in mostly old French barriques, malolactic for part of the wine and long ageing on its lees, so that savour and texture stand where the usual pungency would be. The house makes a classic Sauvignon Blanc beside it, and the two poured side by side show what the barrel changes. For a sommelier, Wild Sauvignon is the proof that Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc is more than one style.

changed.was: The Fromm family makes wine at Malans in Graubünden, in eastern Switzerland, and in the late 1980s a winegrower of that family and a fellow Swiss winemaker resolved to make wine in Marlborough. In 1992, by the house's account, Fromm Winery began with its first harvest, and its founding vineyard was planted that year; in a region turning to Sauvignon Blanc, the house made red grapes its focus, Pinot Noir, Syrah and Malbec. At the end of the Brancott Valley, meanwhile, a viticulturist and his wife had planted Clayvin in the early 1990s, closely spaced on north facing clay slopes, a vineyard often called Marlborough's first commercial hillside planting, and in 1998 they sold it to Fromm. Its Pinot Noir, grown organically, fermented with indigenous yeasts and bottled unfined and unfiltered, became the wine by which the house is known. The founding family returned to Switzerland in 2008, and the estate passed to Swiss partners. In 2015, after a long lease, the Marlborough house of Giesen bought the vineyard, and Fromm has gone on making its Clayvin wines from the site. For a sommelier, Clayvin shows what Marlborough's clay hillsides can give Pinot Noir: grip and depth from a region better known for Sauvignon Blanc.
